 Pediatric Heart Rate Variability Marker Loses Significance After Adjusting for Life Support
 by 
 November 17, 2026

 Health 
 Reading Time: 3 mins read
 0 
 Pediatric Heart Rate Variability Marker Loses Significance After Adjusting for Life Support
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram 
 In deeply sedated, mechanically ventilated children, an autonomic heart rate variability metric known as normalized high-frequency power correlates with multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, yet its statistical link disappears after adjusting for respiratory and vasoactive support. This observation was reported by researchers Ercan Yılmaz and Zeynep Yamancan Yılmaz in a letter to the editor published in the Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing. The authors examined findings by Wojtanowski and colleagues, who evaluated heart rate variability as a continuous bedside signal to detect organ dysfunction in critically ill pediatric patients.
 Normalized high-frequency power, abbreviated as HFnu, was higher in pediatric patients classified as having moderate or severe organ failure compared to those with no or mild dysfunction. This metric discriminated between the two illness categories with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.75. Although this finding supported investigating heart rate variability as a continuous bedside monitor, Yılmaz and Yamancan Yılmaz pointed out that the clinical interpretation warrants scrutiny because the reference standard for organ failure overlaps with conditions altering autonomic variability.
 In the investigated cohort, moderate to severe multiple organ dysfunction syndrome was defined post hoc as a pediatric Sequential Organ Failure Assessment, or pSOFA, score above 5. Notably, the difference in pSOFA scores between the patient cohorts was heavily concentrated in cardiopulmonary components. While neurological and renal subscores did not differ significantly between groups, the cardiovascular and respiratory dimensions accounted for nearly all of the scoring separation.
 The numerical data showed that median cardiovascular and respiratory subscores reached 3 and 4 in the moderate to severe group, compared to 1 and 0 in the mild cohort. Patients with moderate to severe organ dysfunction also required substantially higher levels of medical support. Median fraction of inspired oxygen was 60 percent in the severe group versus 30 percent in the milder group, and catecholamines were administered to 78 percent of severe patients compared to 24 percent of milder patients.
 This imbalance creates an interpretive issue that exceeds standard residual confounding. Oxygenation and vasoactive infusions directly determine the respiratory and cardiovascular components of the pSOFA score, but they also directly affect the physiological environment where autonomic heart rate variability is measured. Because therapy intensity defines the reference category and simultaneously influences autonomic function, isolating the independent meaning of normalized high-frequency power becomes challenging.
 Crucially, the observed link between normalized high-frequency power and multiorgan dysfunction lost statistical significance after separate adjustment for fraction of inspired oxygen or catecholamine administration. Statistical adjustment alone cannot clarify whether the metric reflects systemic dysfunction across multiple organs or simply mirrors intensive cardiopulmonary support. A contemporaneous correlation with pSOFA does not prove that heart rate variability provides actionable insights beyond the severity and treatment state already captured by the score.
 To clarify this distinction, the authors recommend prospective longitudinal research with serial heart rate variability monitoring, a methodology previously applied in pediatric studies. Tracking changes in normalized high-frequency power relative to subsequent pSOFA variations could establish whether autonomic alterations precede worsening organ function or escalation of life support. Demonstrating that heart rate variability shifts occur before respiratory or vasoactive support increases would validate the signal as a prospective early monitor rather than a concurrent reflection of organ injury and intensive therapy.
 Subject of Research: Autonomic heart rate variability and cardiopulmonary support in pediatric multiorgan dysfunction
 Article Title: Does HFnu reflect multiorgan dysfunction or cardiopulmonary support intensity in critically ill children?
